enonce_intro_markdown:
The data on the Table shows the cost and revenue of a hypothetical firm with total costs of 100 FRS. All the figures are in FCFA.

| Output | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Total revenue | 81 | 162 | 243 | 324 | 405 | 486 | 567 |
| Total variable cost | 90 | 170 | 240 | 300 | 350 | 450 | 550 |

Les calculs (coût total, coût marginal, profit, coût variable moyen) sont recalculés par script : production de 5 unités, perte de 45 FCFA, seuil de fermeture 70 FCFA (minimum du coût variable moyen).

Question 3(c)(ii) : « un secteur où les oligopoles dominent » ; le corrigé cite les télécommunications (réponse type, non vérifiée par un chiffre) et d'autres secteurs acceptables, sans statistique. Points imprimés : (a) 6 + 1, (b) 4, (c) 8 + 1, soit 20.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Given that this firm exists in a perfectly competitive industry determine the profit maximization or loss minimization level of output. (6 marks)

(ii) What will be the level of profits in a (i) above? (1 mark)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Output level.** In perfect competition the firm is a price taker: price = average revenue = marginal revenue. From the table, $P = MR = \dfrac{TR}{Q} = \dfrac{81}{1} = 81$ FCFA at every output.

The "total costs of 100" is read as **total fixed cost (TFC) = 100 FCFA**, so $TC = TFC + TVC$. Marginal cost is the extra cost of the last unit, $MC = \Delta TVC = \Delta TC$.

| Output | TR | TVC | TC = TVC + 100 | MC | MR = P | Profit = TR - TC |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 81 | 90 | 190 | 90 | 81 | -109 |
| 2 | 162 | 170 | 270 | 80 | 81 | -108 |
| 3 | 243 | 240 | 340 | 70 | 81 | -97 |
| 4 | 324 | 300 | 400 | 60 | 81 | -76 |
| 5 | 405 | 350 | 450 | 50 | 81 | **-45** |
| 6 | 486 | 450 | 550 | 100 | 81 | -64 |
| 7 | 567 | 550 | 650 | 100 | 81 | -83 |

The firm maximises profit (here minimises loss) where **MR = MC with MC rising**, or, equivalently, at the last unit for which $MC \le MR$. The fifth unit adds 50 FCFA to cost and 81 FCFA to revenue, so it raises profit; the sixth unit adds 100 FCFA to cost but only 81 FCFA to revenue, so it lowers profit. (The first unit has $MC = 90 > MR = 81$ but MC is falling there, so it is not the equilibrium.)

**The profit-maximising (loss-minimising) level of output is 5 units.** At that output the loss is the smallest, 45 FCFA, as the profit column confirms.

**(ii) Level of profit.**

$$
\text{Profit} = TR - TC = 405 - (350 + 100) = 405 - 450 = -45
$$

The firm makes a **loss of 45 FCFA** (an economic loss; it is minimising its loss, not making a profit). The loss is less than the fixed cost of 100 FCFA, which it would lose if it closed down, so it should continue to produce in the short run.

questions.enonce_markdown: Below what price should this firm cease production in the short run. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
In the short run a firm in perfect competition should shut down when the price falls **below the minimum of its average variable cost (AVC)**, because then total revenue does not even cover the variable costs, and it would lose less (only its fixed cost) by closing.

$AVC = \dfrac{TVC}{Q}$:

| Output | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| AVC (FCFA) | 90 | 85 | 80 | 75 | **70** | 75 | 78.57 |

The minimum AVC is **70 FCFA, at 5 units of output**. So the firm should **cease production in the short run if the price falls below 70 FCFA**. At the present price of 81 FCFA, which is above 70 FCFA, it covers its variable cost: $TR - TVC = 405 - 350 = 55$ FCFA is available to pay part of the 100 FCFA of fixed cost, hence the loss of 45 FCFA.

questions.enonce_markdown:
If this firm were transformed to an oligopolist with heavy product branding.

(i) State four ways it will be different from a perfect competitor. (8 marks)

(ii) Name one sector in Cameroon where oligopolists are predominant. (1 mark)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)**

An oligopolist with heavy product branding is one of a few large firms producing differentiated (branded) products. It differs from a perfect competitor in these ways (2 marks each, any four):

1. **Price maker, not price taker.** A perfect competitor faces a horizontal demand curve ($P = AR = MR$) and must accept the market price. The branded oligopolist faces a **downward-sloping demand curve**, so it has some power over price (MR is below AR), and it must lower price to sell more.
2. **Product differentiation.** A perfect competitor sells a homogeneous (identical) product. The oligopolist sells branded products that consumers see as different, which gives it brand loyalty.
3. **Interdependence of firms.** There are few firms, so each must consider the reactions of its rivals when it sets price or output (this explains the kinked demand curve, price rigidity or collusion). A perfect competitor, one among very many, ignores the others.
4. **Non-price competition.** The oligopolist competes through advertising, branding, packaging, after-sales service and promotions. A perfect competitor does not advertise because it can sell all it wants at the market price.
5. **Barriers to entry.** Large economies of scale, brand loyalty and heavy advertising cost make it difficult for new firms to enter, so **supernormal profit can last in the long run**. Perfect competition has free entry and exit, so only normal profit is earned in the long run.
6. **Few, large sellers.** The market is dominated by a handful of large firms, instead of a large number of small firms.

Any four differences, explained, earn the 8 marks.

**(ii)**

One sector of Cameroon where oligopolists are predominant (1 mark): **telecommunications**, where a few mobile network operators dominate the market. Other accepted examples: brewing and soft drinks, cement, banking, petroleum products distribution.
